State of New Jersey
OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
INITIAL DECISION
OAL DKT. NO. TYP 9437-11
AGENCY DKT. NO.
CHRISTOPHER MOUNT,
v.
POLICE AND FIREMEN’S
RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
_________________________
M. Scott Tashjy, Esq., for petitioner (The Tashjy Law Firm, LLC, attorneys)
Joseph F. Dorfler, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (John J. Hoffman, Acting Attorney General of New Jersey,
attorney)
Record Closed: September 19, 2014 Decided: October 31, 2014
BEFORE RONALD W. REBA, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
By letter dated June 14, 2011, the Board of Trustees of the Police and Firemen’s Retirement System notified petitioner
Christopher Mount that the Board found that he is totally and permanently psychiatrically disabled as a direct result of a work-
related incident. However, the Board found that the event in question was not objectively capable of causing a reasonable
person in similar circumstances to suffer a disabling mental injury, as petitioner’s disability did not result from “direct personal
experience of a terrifying or horror-inducing event that involved actual or threatened death or serious injury, or a similarly serious
threat to the physical integrity of the member or another person,” and therefore denied his application for accidental disability.
The Board also found that the event was not undesigned and unexpected. However, as a result of the Board’s finding of
disability, petitioner was granted an ordinary disability retirement. Petitioner appealed the Board’s determination, and the Board
transmitted the matter to the Office of Administrative Law, where on August 9, 2011, it was filed as a contested case. N.J.S.A.
52:14F-1 to -15; N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to -13.

A hearing was conducted on July 10, 2014. Petitioner presented testimony on his own behalf. The Board offered no testimony.
Both parties submitted post hearing briefs, where they presented their arguments. The record closed on September 19, 2014.
FACTUAL DISCUSSION
The essential facts are not in dispute.
3 On January 10, 2007, petitioner was on duty as a patrol officer for the Freehold Township Police Department. He
received a call from his dispatcher which directed him to proceed to a motor vehicle accident on or about Kozloski Road in
Freehold, New Jersey. While en route to the accident scene, Officer Mount was not advised or otherwise made aware of the
specific details of the accident scene or of any injuries. Upon arrival as one of the first officers at the scene, Officer Mount
blocked off traffic, assessed damage and secured the accident scene. Officer Mount came upon a motor vehicle that was
emitting dark, black smoke, and he observed a human arm that he described as a “limb” partially exposed outside the driver’s-
side window of the vehicle. Bystanders were attempting to approach the vehicle, and they were calling to Officer Mount to “do
something” for those trapped in the damaged vehicle. Officer Mount got within one to one and one-half feet from the damaged
vehicle when the vehicle, according to petitioner, “exploded into flames.” Officer Mount testified that the explosion of fire was so
intense that he felt as if his eyelids were going to burn off, and he felt “extreme heat” from his kneecaps to his head, and the
intensity of the heat pushed Officer Mount backwards. He said there was “immense heat,” with flames “billowing” out the
windows of the vehicle. He described that his nose hairs were singed because of the intense heat.
Officer Mount tried to approach the vehicle again, but was unable to get as close as he originally had been because of the
“extreme” heat that he characterized as “unbearable.” Officer Mount testified that he had no protective gear or emergency
devices on his person to assist him in entering the burning motor vehicle, and his motor vehicle also contained no such
emergency equipment. There was a fire extinguisher in his vehicle; however, the size of the fire extinguisher was appropriate for
a brush fire, and he thought it would have been inadequate against the size and intensity of the fire that exploded from the
damaged vehicle. Officer Mount stated that he called for emergency medical personnel, requested more traffic assistance, and
called the fire department. He said that thereafter he could do nothing but observe the burning vehicle and attempt to keep
bystanders away from the vehicle until the fire department arrived. He estimated that he was in close proximity to the burned
vehicle for about ten minutes after the fire was extinguished.
Prior to working as a law enforcement officer for Freehold Township, Officer Mount had been trained at the Monmouth
County Police Academy (Academy) for hire as a sheriff’s officer with the Monmouth County Sheriff’s Department.H e had
generalized law-enforcement training, physical and classroom, training at the Academy, but no outside specialized training. After
leaving the Academy, and upon being hired in his position for Freehold Township in October 1996, Officer Mount was assigned
to a training partner. While at Freehold Township, he took a class called Method of Instruction, which taught him how to teach
recruits the proper way to conduct a motor vehicle stop. Mount later taught a class at the Academy on motor vehicle stops, which
included regular safety procedures and felony stops. He was not required to undergo, and did not receive, any formal
supplemental training regarding how to extract injured victims from motor vehicles following an accident or how to extract victims
from motor vehicles engulfed by fire, and no specific training as to how to assist victims in fire-related incidents. Officer Mount
explained that with regard to attending to victims in motor-vehicle accidents, his job was to “back up” or assist emergency
medical personnel in rendering assistance to victims.
Prior to the incident of January 10, 2007, Officer Mount had been involved in responding to one fatal accident; he was
involved in responding to two more after this incident. He also had observed accident scenes where victims needed to be

“extracted” from a damaged motor vehicle. The extractions were performed by the fire department. He confirmed that the fire
department removed the bodies of three victims of the January 10, 2007, accident; he was directing traffic during that time. He
said that he could smell the odor of burnt flesh, and that he had never before, in all his years on the force in Freehold Township,
encountered a motor-vehicle fire involving live victims or victims who were burned to death. Officer Mount testified that he
observed the remains of three teenagers after the fire was extinguished, which he said were unrecognizable melted, charred
bodies. He testified that the photographs taken by the Freehold Township Police Department as part of the fatality investigation
at the accident scene (P-1) accurately represented exactly what he saw after the fire was extinguished, and what the remains of
the victims looked like.
On cross-examination, Mount acknowledged that it was part of his job duties to protect accident scenes from possible
disturbances. It was also his job duty to remove or assist in removing deceased individuals from wreckage.
On questioning by this judge, petitioner was confronted with a report of the incident prepared by Freehold police officer
George Burdge, which stated that a bystander had attempted to put out the vehicle fire with a fire extinguisher; however, Mount
could not recall that happening. First petitioner said that it might have happened before he got to the scene. Then he said that it
might have happened after he got to the scene, despite his being with the car until the fire was put out, as he had testified.
Petitioner acknowledged that even though this event took place in 2007, it was not until 2009 that he began to realize he
was having problems. He was abusing alcohol, and ultimately entered a rehabilitation program and underwent successful
treatment. He went back to work, but was still troubled, and in 2010 he was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder by a
psychiatrist. He filed for accidental disability with a retirement date of December 1, 2010.
Officer Mount confirmed that when he joined the Freehold Township Police Department he was told that he could expect
to be involved with the aftermath of motor-vehicle accidents.
LEGAL ANALYSIS
1In most causes of action, whether judicial or administrative, the party asserting a claim has the burden to prove it. WCI-
Westinghouse, Inc. v. Edison Tp., 7 N.J. Tax 610, 630 (Tax Ct. 1985), aff’d, 9 N.J. Tax 86 (App. Div. 1986). An applicant for
benefits is the proponent in an eligibility determination and therefore must shoulder the burden of proof. Stein, Mitchell, Mezines
Administrative Law §24.02 (2002). Therefore, in order for petitioner to prevail, he must prove by a preponderance of the
evidence that he experienced a terrifying or horror inducing event and that the incident of January 10, 2007, was undesigned and
unexpected. See In re Polk License Revocation, 90 N.J. 550 (1982).
3 N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7(1) provides that
[u]pon the written application by a member in service . . . any member may be retired on an
accidental disability retirement allowance; provided, that the medical board, after a medical
examination of such member, shall certify that the member is permanently and totally disabled as a
direct result of a traumatic event occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or
assigned duties and that such disability was not the result of the member’s willful negligence and that
such member is mentally or physically incapacitated for the performance of his usual duty and of any
other available duty in the department which his employer is willing to assign to him.
In Richardson v. Board of Trustees, Police and Firemen’s Retirement System, 192 N.J. 189, 212–13 (2007), the

Supreme Court determined that the above language creates a multi-pronged test:
. . . [A] traumatic event is essentially the same as what we historically understood an accident to be
—an unexpected external happening that directly causes injury and is not the result of pre-existing
disease alone or in combination with work effort. Thus, to obtain accidental disability benefits, a
member must prove:
1. that he is permanently and totally disabled;
2. as a direct result of a traumatic event that is
a. identifiable as to time and place,
b. undesigned and unexpected, and
c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease
that is aggravated or accelerated by the work);
3. that the traumatic event occurred during and as a result of the member’s regular or assigned
duties;
4. that the disability was not the result of the member’s willful negligence; and
5. that the member is mentally or physically incapacitated from performing his usual or any other
duty.
In this case, the disputed prong of the test is 2(b), whether petitioner is disabled as a result of a traumatic event that was
“undesigned and unexpected.”
To qualify for accidental disability benefits based on a mental injury, in addition to satisfying the requirements set forth in
Richardson, an applicant must show that his disability resulted from “direct personal experience of a terrifying or horror-inducing
event that involves actual or threatened death or serious injury.” Patterson v. Bd. of Trs., State Police Ret. Sys,. 194 N.J. 29, 34
(2008). The terrifying-or-horror-inducing-event standard ensures that the event is “not inconsequential but is objectively capable
of causing a reasonable person in similar circumstances to suffer a disabling mental injury.” Id. at 34.
In Russo v. Board of Trustees, Police and Firemen’s Retirement System, 206 N.J. 14 (2011), a first-year police officer
entered a burning building to save trapped victims. The Board found that although Russo experienced a terrifying and horror-
inducing event, the experience was not “objectively capable of causing a disabling mental injury to a reasonable person in
similar circumstances” and denied him accidental disability benefits. However, the Russo Court clarified that the objective-
reasonableness standard of Patterson is met once the employee experiences a qualifying horrific event. Thus, once the member
experiences a terrifying or horror-inducing event, Patterson is satisfied and the member must then demonstrate the further
criteria as set forth in Richardson. Examples of terrifying or horror-inducing events provided in Patterson include: a policeman
who sees his partner shot; a teacher who is held hostage by a student; and a government lawyer used as a shield by a

defendant. Patterson, supra, 194 N.J. at 50.
In Russo, the Court found that the officer experienced a terrifying or horror-inducing event. This was based on Russo
being ordered into a burning building that was so hot and full of smoke and fire that his uniform was singed and he became
nauseous and disoriented. He was still in his first year on the force. He was terrified, could not breathe, could not see, and could
not believe what was happening. Russo eventually had to be escorted out by the firemen who later arrived. Russo was
hospitalized that night due to smoke inhalation. The Court highlighted that Russo did not have any training or equipment to enter
a burning building in this fashion. Further, Russo observed one of the victims he attempted to rescue being carried out of the
house after dying inside. The victim’s family confronted Russo and blamed him for the death.
The petitioner’s experience on January 10, 2007, involved witnessing a scene in which three teenagers burned to death,
smelling burning flesh, hearing concerned bystanders screaming for him to “do something,” and having inadequate equipment to
assist the victims. I CONCLUDE that this event meets the Patterson test.
However, Patterson requires that in order for accidental disability to be granted, the disability must result from the
terrifying or horror-inducing experience. I cannot find that the petitioner’s disability was solely and directly related to his
experience with the incident in question. Petitioner testified that he directed traffic after witnessing the scene of the accident, and
that he continued to work without a problem until some two years later. He conceded that in 2009 he was dealing with alcohol
abuse and other personal problems. He acknowledged that he had witnessed at least one fatality before the 2007 incident, as
well as other horrific car accidents where individuals were severely injured. There was no direct link shown between the incident
of January 10, 2007, and petitioner’s disability.
The remaining issue is whether the event was “undesigned and unexpected.” The Russo Court explains that
an employee who experiences a horrific event which falls within his job description and for which he
has been trained will be unlikely to pass the “undesigned and unexpected” test. Thus, for example,
an emergency medical technician who comes upon a terrible accident involving life-threatening
injuries or death, will have experienced a Patterson-type horrific event, but will not satisfy
Richardson’s “undesigned and unexpected” standard because that is exactly what his training has
prepared him for.
[Russo, supra, 206 N.J. at 33.]
I agree with respondent that unlike in Russo, Mount’s training and experience had prepared him for this event, rendering it
not undesigned and unexpected. Police officers are first responders, and as such are routinely called upon to respond to
emergency situations, and, by definition, some of those situations are stressful. Police officers are required to respond to such
emergencies as house fires, motor-vehicle accidents, domestic-violence incidents and grisly crime scenes.
Mount’s job description states that he is to secure motor-vehicle-accident scenes. A police officer may also be tasked to
remove dead or injured individuals from wreckage. Thus, responding to accidents, including fatal motor-vehicle accidents, was
part of his job description. Mount also learned through his training officer the protocol for approaching motor-vehicle-crash
scenes. He was to assess traffic, block off any potential disturbances, then assist the parties involved and process the scene.
This is precisely what he did. He blocked off traffic with his patrol car, ran to the car on fire, and then protected the bystanders by
getting them away from the wreckage.

Petitioner acknowledged that he had responded to other fatal car accidents, as well as accidents involving serious bodily
injuries requiring the “jaws of life,” as part of his duties as a police officer. He also had responded to accident scenes where cars
were engulfed in flames. In none of the other incidents was he involved in either rescuing the victims or fighting the fires. Mount
attempted to distinguish these other events by saying that he had never seen a fatal car accident in which the vehicle was also
on fire. However, an event is not undesigned and unexpected only because it was his first time. I agree with respondent that
responding to such accident scenes falls squarely within petitioner’s job description and training and, thus, I CONCLUDE that
the incident of January 10, 2007, was not undesigned and unexpected.
Therefore, based on the above, I CONCLUDE that the petitioner is not eligible for accidental disability retirement benefits.
ORDER
It is ORDERED that petitioner’s application for an accidental disability retirement is hereby DENIED.
I hereby FILE my initial decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND FIREMEN’S RETIREMENT
SYSTEM for consideration.
This recommended decision may be adopted, modified or rejected by the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND
FIREMEN’S RETIREMENT SYSTE, Mwhich by law is authorized to make a final decision in this matter. If the Board of
Trustees of the Police and Firemen’s Retirement System does not adopt, modify or reject this decision within forty five days and
unless such time limit is otherwise extended, this recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with
N.J.S.A. 52:14B 10.
Within thirteen days from the date on which this recommended decision was mailed to the parties, any party may file written
exceptions with the DIRECTOR, DIVISION OF PENSIONS, One State Street Square, 50 West State Street, PO Box 295,
